==Problem==

The line <math>12x+5y=60</math> forms a triangle with the coordinate axes. What is the sum of the lengths of the altitudes of this triangle?

<math>\textbf{(A) } 20 \qquad\textbf{(B) } \dfrac{360}{17} \qquad\textbf{(C) } \dfrac{107}{5} \qquad\textbf{(D) } \dfrac{43}{2} \qquad\textbf{(E) } \dfrac{281}{13} </math>

==Solution 1==
We find the <math>x</math>-intercepts and the <math>y</math>-intercepts to find the intersections of the axes and the line. If <math>x=0</math>, then <math>y=12</math>. If <math>y</math> is <math>0</math>, then <math>x=5</math>. Our three vertices are <math>(0,0)</math>, <math>(5,0)</math>, and <math>(0,12)</math>. Two of our altitudes are <math>5</math> and <math>12</math>, and since it is a <math>5</math>-<math>12</math>-<math>13</math> right triangle, the hypotenuse is <math>13</math>. Since the area of the triangle is <math>30</math>, so our final altitude is <math>\frac{30(2)}{13}=\frac{60}{13}</math>. The sum of our altitudes is <math>\frac{60+156+65}{13}=\boxed{\textbf{(E)} \dfrac{281}{13}}</math>. Note that there is no need to calculate the final answer after we know that the third altitude has length <math>\frac{60}{13}</math> since <math>E</math> is the only choice with a denominator of <math>13</math> and <math>13</math> is relatively prime to <math>5</math> and <math>12</math>.

==Solution 2 (very similar to Solution 1)==
Noticing that the line has coefficients <imath>12</imath> and <imath>5</imath>, we can suspect that we have a <imath>5</imath>-<imath>12</imath>-<imath>13</imath> triangle on our hands. Because we want the sum of the altitudes, the third altitude that is not an axis must have a denominator of <imath>13</imath>. Since the other altitudes are integers, we choose the option with <imath>13</imath> as the denominator, namely <imath>E</imath>.

==Solution 3 (point to line distance formula)==
Similar to the above solutions, we find that the three vertices of the triangle are <imath>(0, 0)</imath>, <imath>(0, 12)</imath>, and <imath>(5, 0)</imath>.
We already know the length of two of the altitudes (12 and 5 respectively). To find the third altitude we use the formula for a point to a line:

<imath>d = \frac{|Ax_0 + By_0 + C|}{\sqrt{A^2 + B^2}}</imath> for the point <imath>(x_0, y_0)</imath> and the line in the form of <imath>Ax + By + C = 0</imath>.

Using this formula we plug in the known values:
<cmath>d = \frac{|12 \cdot 0 + 5 \cdot 0 - 60|}{\sqrt{12^2 + 5^2}}</cmath>
<cmath>d = \frac{|-60|}{\sqrt{169}}</cmath>
<cmath>d = \frac{60}{13}</cmath>

At this point, we are likely already able to guess that the answer choice is <imath>\frac{281}{13}</imath>, because it is the only choice with the denominator being 13. But, we can still confirm this, just in case, by summing up the three heights:
<cmath>12 + 5 + \frac{60}{13} = \frac{156}{13} + \frac{65}{13} + \frac{60}{13} = \boxed{\frac{281}{13}}</cmath>

~Kellan Zhang (ThePlenGuy)
